query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In solidified, Co‐free FeNiCrMn, the dynamic mechanical response is governed by a rate‐dependent transition between thermally activated dislocation glide (which produces stacking faults and enables ductility) and a phonon‐drag dominated dislocation motion (which increases flow stress and reduces ductility) as temperature and strain rate vary.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Co‐free FeNiCrMn produced by solidification, exhibiting an FCC-dominated microstructure with controlled grain boundaries and low initial defect density.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to both tensile and compressive dynamic deformation tests at varied temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 900 K) and a range of strain rates (from quasi-static ~10⁻³ s⁻¹ to dynamic ~10³ s⁻¹).
generation.conditions: Samples prepared with uniform microstructure and grain size, ensuring that comparisons across test conditions are made on materials with similar defect states and phase distributions.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution and interplay of stacking faults and dislocation densities; specifically, the extent of stacking fault formation versus dislocation entanglement mediates the transition between ductile and high-strength responses.
generation.mechanism: At low strain rates and higher temperatures, thermal energy promotes dislocation glide that is accommodated by forming stacking faults, enabling higher ductility. At high strain rates (and/or lower temperatures), the limited time for thermal activation enhances the influence of phonon drag, causing dislocation motion to slow down and accumulate, which raises the flow stress and reduces ductility. This switch in dominant mechanisms is what governs the dynamic behavior and maintains the unique strength–ductility balance in FeNiCrMn.
generation.predicted_outcome: Experiments will reveal a clear transition: under low strain rate/high temperature conditions, the material will show lower flow stress, extensive stacking fault formation, and greater plastic deformation, while under high strain rate/low temperature conditions, higher flow stress and increased dislocation entanglement with less stacking fault recovery will predominate.
generation.baseline: The mechanical response measured under quasi-static deformation at room temperature, where thermally activated dislocation glide is the primary mechanism, serves as the baseline.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for Co‐free FeNiCrMn solidified under controlled conditions with an FCC-dominated microstructure; deviations may occur if there are significant variations in grain size, chemical ordering, or if secondary phases/defects dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative shift between thermally activated dislocation motion and phonon drag is supported by previous studies in related systems, the precise strain rate and temperature thresholds, as well as the quantitative contributions of stacking fault formation versus dislocation entanglement, require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of Co‐free FeNiCrMn samples with tightly controlled initial microstructure. Deform the samples in both tension and compression across a matrix of temperatures (e.g., 77 K, 300 K, 900 K) and strain rates (from 10⁻³ s⁻¹ to 10³ s⁻¹). Utilize in-situ high-resolution characterization techniques (e.g., TEM with real-time diffraction imaging, digital image correlation) to monitor dislocation nucleation, stacking fault evolution, and any phase transformations.
measurements: Dislocation density and stacking fault fraction via microscopy/analysis
Phase and microstructure identification through diffraction techniques
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental data do not show a consistent shift from a thermally activated, stacking fault-mediated mechanism at low strain rates/high temperatures to a phonon-drag limited, dislocation entanglement-dominated mechanism at high strain rates/low temperatures – that is, if the changes in flow stress and microstructural indicators do not correlate with the predicted trends – then the hypothesis is falsified.
